reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Splenic abscess is uncommon but important, and classically presents with fever, left upper quadrant pain, and left-sided tenderness, sometimes with referred left shoulder-tip pain
It most often arises from haematogenous seeding, with infective endocarditis a notable source, and is increasingly seen in immunocompromised and diabetic patients
A left pleural effusion, basal atelectasis, or raised hemidiaphragm may be present and can distract from the underlying splenic pathology
Contrast CT is the imaging modality of choice and defines the size, number, and character of collections, while ultrasound is a useful bedside adjunct
Blood cultures and identification of the causative organism guide targeted antimicrobial therapy; polymicrobial, fungal (especially Candida in the immunosuppressed), and mycobacterial causes occur

Management combines appropriate antibiotics with drainage; image-guided percutaneous drainage may suffice for a unilocular collection, while splenectomy is often required for multiloculated or refractory disease
An untreated or ruptured splenic abscess can lead to overwhelming sepsis, so prompt diagnosis and source control are essential
reference.pathophysiology: Splenic abscesses develop when organisms reach and proliferate within splenic tissue, most commonly by haematogenous spread from a distant focus such as infective endocarditis, or from contiguous infection, penetrating trauma, or infarction of the spleen (as in sickle cell disease) that subsequently becomes infected. Immunosuppression, diabetes, and intravenous drug use increase susceptibility and broaden the range of pathogens to include fungi and unusual bacteria. Localised suppuration forms a walled-off collection of pus; as it enlarges it can rupture into the peritoneal cavity, causing peritonitis, or into adjacent structures, and can seed the bloodstream to produce systemic sepsis.
additionalDifferentials: Splenic cyst (including hydatid cyst) or pseudocyst
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to characterise the abscess
Blood cultures and inflammatory markers to identify the organism and monitor response
Echocardiography to seek infective endocarditis as a source
Ultrasound for bedside assessment and to guide percutaneous drainage
Aspirate microscopy, culture, and sensitivity from drained material
Screening for immunocompromise (including HIV and diabetes) where relevant
redFlags: Signs of rupture with peritonitis and haemodynamic instability requiring emergency surgery
Septic shock or multi-organ dysfunction from uncontrolled infection
Rapid clinical deterioration despite antibiotics indicating inadequate source control
Underlying infective endocarditis with ongoing embolic risk
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, effective antimicrobial therapy, and adequate drainage or splenectomy the outlook is generally favourable. Mortality rises sharply with delayed treatment, rupture, multiloculated or fungal infection, and significant immunocompromise. After splenectomy patients require lifelong precautions and vaccination against encapsulated organisms.
pitfalls: Attributing left upper quadrant pain and fever to pneumonia or a pleural effusion and missing the splenic source
Relying on antibiotics alone for a large or multiloculated abscess that requires drainage
Failing to seek and treat an underlying source such as endocarditis
Neglecting post-splenectomy sepsis prophylaxis and vaccination
Overlooking fungal or atypical organisms in immunocompromised patients
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Prompt empirical intravenous antibiotics covering enteric Gram-negatives, anaerobes and streptococci, then narrowed to blood and aspirate culture and sensitivities
Add antifungal cover with an echinocandin or azole where Candida is likely, as in the immunocompromised, and antituberculous therapy if a mycobacterial cause is confirmed
Drainage of the collection: image-guided percutaneous drainage for a unilocular abscess, with splenectomy for multiloculated or refractory disease
Source control by identifying and treating the origin, notably infective endocarditis, using echocardiography and appropriately prolonged therapy
Resuscitation and sepsis management with fluids and haemodynamic support, and urgent laparotomy with splenectomy for rupture causing peritonitis
Monitor clinical response, inflammatory markers and repeat imaging to confirm resolution
After splenectomy, give pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b immunisation plus antibiotic prophylaxis, and counsel on overwhelming post-splenectomy infection
